↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ROBBERY Practised by the Ishmaelites (Genesis 16:12), the Chaldeans and Sabeans (Job 1:15, 17), and the men of Shechem (Judges 9:25. See also 1 Samuel 27:6-10; 30; Hos. 4:2; 6:9). Robbers infested Judea in our Lord’s time (Luke 10:30; John 18:40; Acts 5:36, 37; 21:38; 2 Corinthians 11:26). The words of the Authorized Version, “counted it not robbery to be equal,” etc. (Phil. 2:6, 7), are better rendered in the Revised Version, “counted it not a prize to be on an equality,” etc., i.e., “did not look upon equality with God as a prize which must not slip from his grasp” = “did not cling with avidity to the prerogatives of his divine majesty; did not ambitiously display his equality with God.” “Robbers of churches” should be rendered, as in the Revised Version, “of temples.” In the temple at Ephesus there was a great treasure-chamber, and as all that was laid up there was under the guardianship of the goddess Diana, to steal from such a place would be sacrilege (Acts 19:37).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee'. Ephrem reads the divine name-change as a SACRAMENTAL renaming: the addition of the heh (the divine breath / spirit-letter, also added to Sarai → Sarah) signifies the entry of the divine name itself into Abraham's identity. Tewahedo baptismal liturgy preserves the name-given-at-baptism tradition (the newly-baptised receives a Christian saint-name) as the sacramental continuation of this Abrahamic name-change pattern.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FEAST as a mark of hospitality (Genesis 19:3; 2 Samuel 3:20; 2 Kings 6:23); on occasions of domestic joy (Luke 15:23; Genesis 21:8); on birthdays (Genesis 40:20; Job 1:4; Matthew 14:6); and on the occasion of a marriage (Judges 14:10; Genesis 29:22). Feasting was a part of the observances connected with the offering up of sacrifices (Deuteronomy 12:6, 7; 1 Samuel 9:19; 16:3, 5), and with the annual festivals (Deuteronomy 16:11). “It was one of the designs of the greater solemnities, which required the attendance of the people at the sacred tent, that the oneness of the nation might be maintained and cemented together, by statedly congregating in one place, and with one soul taking part in the same religious services. But that oneness was primarily and chiefly a religious and not merely a political one; the people were not merely to meet as among themselves, but with Jehovah, and to present themselves before him as one body; the meeting was in its own nature a binding of themselves in fellowship with Jehovah; so that it was not politics and commerce that had here to do, but the soul of the Mosaic dispensation, the foundation of the religious and political existence of Israel, the covenant with Jehovah. To keep the people’s consciousness alive to this, to revive, strengthen, and perpetuate it, nothing could be so well adapated as these annual feasts.” (See FESTIVALS.)

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

Isaac's birth: the Lord visited Sarah as He had said. Ephrem reads the laughter motif (Isaac = yiṣḥaq, 'he laughs') as the joy of fulfilled promise: previous laughter (17:17, 18:12) was incredulous; the laughter encoded in Isaac's name is the joy that follows fulfilment. Tewahedo Marian theology preserves this distinction: Mary's response to annunciation moves from troubled wonder (Lk 1:29) to joyful Magnificat (Lk 1:46-55) — the same incredulity-to-joy pattern.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Yitzḥaq (יִצְחָק) — "he laughs." Sarah’s play on Isaac’s name closes a thread of laughter running through the Abraham cycle: Abraham laughed at the promise (17:17), Sarah laughed at the messengers (18:12), and now both laugh in joy. The Hebrew root tz-ḥ-q threads three different laughs — incredulous, derisive, joyful — into the patriarchal narrative.

↩ ◇ Note "We will return." Abraham speaks in the plural — both will return — in defiance of what he believes God has commanded. Hebrews 11:19 reads this as Abraham’s faith that God could raise Isaac from the dead. Jewish midrash explores the same plural at length. The Akedah (binding of Isaac) is one of the most theologically loaded chapters in scripture; in Jewish liturgy it is read at Rosh Hashanah, framing the New Year.

↩ ◇ Note Yahweh-Yireh. The site-name Adonai Yireh ("Yahweh sees" or "Yahweh provides," Hebrew r-’-h functioning ambiguously) commemorates the substitution of the ram for Isaac. The Hebrew root pun runs through the chapter — Abraham earlier said God would "see/provide" (yireh, 22:8) the lamb; the moment of provision becomes the place-name. The mountain is identified in 2 Chr 3:1 as Mount Moriah, the eventual temple-mount; rabbinic tradition (with strong textual support) reads the Akedah (the binding of Isaac) as foundational sacrifice-site for the entire Jerusalem cult. The chapter as a whole is one of the OT’s most theologically demanding texts — Kierkegaard’s Fear and Trembling, Erich Auerbach’s Mimesis, and Levinas’s readings of the Akedah have made the chapter central to modern philosophy of religion. The verse establishes the foundational principle: Yahweh provides at the moment of impossibility. The principle becomes one of the OT’s structuring theological premises — provision arrives precisely at the point at which human resource has been exhausted.

↩ ◇ Note Oath by self. Yahweh swears by himself — the only being greater than whom there is none. Hebrews 6:13–18 develops this verse extensively: God’s oath-by-self provides “two unchangeable things” (promise + oath) by which it is impossible for God to lie. The covenant’s certainty rests not on any external guarantor but on God’s own being. The verse is cited in Jewish liturgy (the daily morning blessings) and underlies the theological claim that covenant promise is unconditional from God’s side.

↩ ◇ Note The death of Sarah. Sarah is the only matriarch whose age at death is recorded (127 years). Rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 58:1) sees the placement after the Akedah as causally linked: Sarah died from grief upon hearing of the binding. The juxtaposition of Akedah and death frames Genesis’s most sustained meditation on mortality. Sarah’s age — 127 — has been read symbolically (e.g., 100 + 20 + 7, three perfect numbers) by traditional commentators.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ARAM-NAHARAIM Aram of the two rivers, is Mesopotamia (as it is rendered in Genesis 24:10), the country enclosed between the Tigris on the east and the Euphrates on the west (Psalm 60, title); called also the “field of Aram” (Hos. 12:12, R.V.) i.e., the open country of Aram; in the Authorized Version, “country of Syria.” Padan-aram (q.v.) was a portion of this country.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MESOPOTAMIA the country between the two rivers (Hebrews Aram-naharaim; i.e., “Syria of the two rivers”), the name given by the Greeks and Romans to the region between the Euphrates and the Tigris (Genesis 24:10; Deuteronomy 23:4; Judges 3:8, 10). In the Old Testament it is mentioned also under the name “Padan-aram;” i.e., the plain of Aram, or Syria (Genesis 25:20). The northern portion of this fertile plateau was the original home of the ancestors of the Hebrews (Genesis 11; Acts 7:2). From this region Isaac obtained his wife Rebecca (Genesis 24:10, 15), and here also Jacob sojourned (28:2-7) and obtained his wives, and here most of his sons were born (35:26; 46:15). The petty, independent tribes of this region, each under its own prince, were warlike, and used chariots in battle. They maintained their independence till after the time of David, when they fell under the dominion of Assyria, and were absorbed into the empire (2 Kings 19:13).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SYRIA (Hebrews Aram), the name in the Old Testament given to the whole country which lay to the north-east of Phoenicia, extending to beyond the Euphrates and the Tigris. Mesopotamia is called (Genesis 24:10; Deuteronomy 23:4) Aram-naharain (=Syria of the two rivers), also Padan-aram (Genesis 25:20). Other portions of Syria were also known by separate names, as Aram-maahah (1 Chronicles 19:6), Aram-beth-rehob (2 Samuel 10:6), Aram-zobah (2 Samuel 10:6, 8). All these separate little kingdoms afterwards became subject to Damascus. In the time of the Romans, Syria included also a part of Palestine and Asia Minor. “From the historic annals now accessible to us, the history of Syria may be divided into three periods: The first, the period when the power of the Pharaohs was dominant over the fertile fields or plains of Syria and the merchant cities of Tyre and Sidon, and when such mighty conquerors as Thothmes III. and Rameses II. could claim dominion and levy tribute from the nations from the banks of the Euphrates to the borders of the Libyan desert. Second, this was followed by a short period of independence, when the Jewish nation in the south was growing in power, until it reached its early zenith in the golden days of Solomon; and when Tyre and Sidon were rich cities, sending their traders far and wide, over land and sea, as missionaries of civilization, while in the north the confederate tribes of the Hittites held back the armies of the kings of Assyria. The third, and to us most interesting, period is that during which the kings of Assyria were dominant over the plains of Syria; when Tyre, Sidon, Ashdod, and Jerusalem bowed beneath the conquering armies of Shalmaneser, Sargon, and Sennacherib; and when at last Memphis and Thebes yielded to the power of the rulers of Nineveh and Babylon, and the kings of Assyria completed with terrible fulness the bruising of the reed of Egypt so clearly foretold by the Hebrew prophets.”, Boscawen.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DEBORAH a bee. (1.) Rebekah’s nurse. She accompanied her mistress when she left her father’s house in Padan-aram to become the wife of Isaac (Genesis 24:59). Many years afterwards she died at Bethel, and was buried under the “oak of weeping”, Allon-bachuth (35:8). (2.) A prophetess, “wife” (woman?) of Lapidoth. Jabin, the king of Hazor, had for twenty years held Israel in degrading subjection. The spirit of patriotism seemed crushed out of the nation. In this emergency Deborah roused the people from their lethargy. Her fame spread far and wide. She became a “mother in Israel” (Judges 4:6, 14; 5:7), and “the children of Israel came up to her for judgment” as she sat in her tent under the palm tree “between Ramah and Bethel.” Preparations were everywhere made by her direction for the great effort to throw off the yoke of bondage. She summoned Barak from Kadesh to take the command of 10,000 men of Zebulun and Naphtali, and lead them to Mount Tabor on the plain of Esdraelon at its north-east end. With his aid she organized this army. She gave the signal for attack, and the Hebrew host rushed down impetuously upon the army of Jabin, which was commanded by Sisera, and gained a great and decisive victory. The Canaanitish army almost wholly perished. That was a great and ever-memorable day in Israel. In Judges 5 is given the grand triumphal ode, the “song of Deborah,” which she wrote in grateful commemoration of that great deliverance. (See LAPIDOTH, JABIN [2].)

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Isaac brought her into his mother Sarah's tent, and took Rebekah, and she became his wife; and he loved her: and Isaac was comforted after his mother's death'. Ephrem reads the marriage as the comfort-in-grief pattern: legitimate human relationships are God's gift FOR consolation. The narrative pattern (find-bride → marry → be-comforted) is preserved in Tewahedo marital theology as the SAFEGUARD against monastic over-spiritualisation: not everyone is called to monastic celibacy; marriage too is sanctifying.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Husbands, Should serve, Tents, Woman.

↩ ◇ Note. Marriage as consolation. One of the most tender lines in the Pentateuch — and one of the few mentions of grief in Genesis. The text’s economy is striking: Sarah’s death gets a full chapter (23); Isaac’s grief gets a single verse, healed by marriage. Rebecca becomes the matriarch by stepping into Sarah’s tent, the household passing mother-to-wife.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ABRAHAM, ABRAHAM, GENEALOGY, KETURAH, MIDIANITES.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KETURAH incense, the wife of Abraham, whom he married probably after Sarah’s death (Genesis 25:1-6), by whom he had six sons, whom he sent away into the east country. Her nationality is unknown. She is styled “Abraham’s concubine” (1 Chronicles 1:32). Through the offshoots of the Keturah line Abraham became the “father of many nations.”

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Midianites.

↩ ◇ Note Keturah and Abraham’s continued line. Abraham’s third wife (after Sarah and Hagar) bears six sons, ancestors of Arab tribes (Sheba, Midian, etc.). The narrative placement after Sarah’s death and before Abraham’s death raises chronological puzzles — by 25:7 Abraham is 175. Rabbinic tradition (Bereshit Rabbah 61:4) identifies Keturah with Hagar reunited; modern critical scholarship treats her as a separate tradition layered into the narrative. The sons of Keturah become eponymous ancestors of various trans-Jordanian and Arabian peoples — connecting Abraham to the broader Semitic world.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ABRAHAM, GENEALOGY, ISHBAK, JOKSHAN, KETURAH.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BILDAD son of contention, one of Job’s friends. He is called “the Shuhite,” probably as belonging to Shuah, a district in Arabia, in which Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah, settled (Genesis 25:2). He took part in each of the three controversies into which Job’s friends entered with him (Job 8:1; 18:1; 25:1), and delivered three speeches, very severe and stern in their tone, although less violent than those of Zophar, but more so than those of Eliphaz.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EPHAH gloom. (1.) One of the five sons of Midian, and grandson of Abraham (Genesis 25:4). The city of Ephah, to which he gave his name, is mentioned Isaiah 60:6, 7. This city, with its surrounding territory, formed part of Midian, on the east shore of the Dead Sea. It abounded in dromedaries and camels (Judges 6:5). (2.) 1 Chronicles 2:46, a concubine of Caleb. (3.) 1 Chronicles 2:47, a descendant of Judah. Ephah, a word of Egyptian origin, meaning measure; a grain measure containing “three seahs or ten omers,” and equivalent to the bath for liquids (Exodus 16:36; 1 Samuel 17:17; Zechariah 5:6). The double ephah in Proverbs 20:10 (marg., “an ephah and an ephah”), Deuteronomy 25:14, means two ephahs, the one false and the other just.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). EPHER a calf. (1.) One of the sons of Midian, who was Abraham’s son by Keturah (Genesis 25:4). (2.) The head of one of the families of trans-Jordanic Manasseh who were carried captive by Tiglath-pileser (1 Chronicles 5:24).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah'. Ephrem dwells on this verse: the half-brothers, Isaac and Ishmael — elsewhere divided — UNITE to bury their father. Ephrem reads this as the eschatological reconciliation of estranged peoples: even when the narrative diverges them, at the threshold of death and burial there is reunion. Tewahedo missiological tradition (the Ethiopian Christian engagement with the Islamic world, including the medieval Solomonic diplomacy with Mamluk Egypt) draws on this verse as canonical witness that descendants-of-Abraham reconciliation is possible.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BURIAL The first burial we have an account of is that of Sarah (Genesis 23). The first commercial transaction recorded is that of the purchase of a burial-place, for which Abraham weighed to Ephron “four hundred shekels of silver current money with the merchants.” Thus the patriarch became the owner of a part of the land of Canaan, the only part he ever possessed. When he himself died, “his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of Machpelah,” beside Sarah his wife (Genesis 25:9). Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, was buried under Allon-bachuth, “the oak of weeping” (Genesis 35:8), near to Bethel. Rachel died, and was buried near Ephrath; “and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave” (16-20). Isaac was buried at Hebron, where he had died (27, 29). Jacob, when charging his sons to bury him in the cave of Machpelah, said, “There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah” (49:31). In compliance with the oath which he made him swear unto him (47:29-31), Joseph, assisted by his brethren, buried Jacob in the cave of Machpelah (50:2, 13). At the Exodus, Moses “took the bones of Joseph with him,” and they were buried in the “parcel of ground” which Jacob had bought of the sons of Hamor (Joshua 24:32), which became Joseph’s inheritance (Genesis 48:22; 1 Chronicles 5:1; John 4:5). Two burials are mentioned as having taken place in the wilderness. That of Miriam (Numbers 20:1), and that of Moses, “in the land of Moab” (Deuteronomy 34:5, 6, 8). There is no account of the actual burial of Aaron, which probably, however, took place on the summit of Mount Hor (Numbers 20:28, 29). Joshua was buried “in the border of his inheritance in Timnath-serah” (Joshua 24: 30). In Job we find a reference to burying-places, which were probably the Pyramids (3:14, 15). The Hebrew word for “waste places” here resembles in sound the Egyptian word for “pyramids.” Samuel, like Moses, was honoured with a national burial (1 Samuel 25:1). Joab (1 Kings 2:34) “was buried in his own house in the wilderness.” In connection with the burial of Saul and his three sons we meet for the first time with the practice of burning the dead (1 Samuel 31:11-13). The same practice is again referred to by Amos (6:10). Absalom was buried “in the wood” where he was slain (2 Samuel 18:17, 18). The raising of the heap of stones over his grave was intended to mark abhorrence of the person buried (comp. Joshua 7:26 and 8:29). There was no fixed royal burying-place for the Hebrew kings. We find several royal burials taking place, however, “in the city of David” (1 Kings 2:10; 11:43; 15:8; 2 Kings 14:19, 20; 15:38; 1 Kings 14:31; 22:50; 2 Chronicles 21:19, 20; 2 Chronicles 24:25, etc.). Hezekiah was buried in the mount of the sepulchres of the sons of David; “and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death” (2 Chronicles 32:33). Little is said regarding the burial of the kings of Israel. Some of them were buried in Samaria, the capital of their kingdom (2 Kings 10:35; 13:9; 14:16). Our Lord was buried in a new tomb, hewn out of the rock, which Joseph of Arimathea had prepared for himself (Matthew 27:57-60; Mark 15:46; John 19:41, 42). The grave of Lazarus was “a cave, and a stone lay on it” (John 11:38). Graves were frequently either natural caverns or artificial excavations formed in the sides of rocks (Genesis 23:9; Matthew 27:60); and coffins were seldom used, unless when the body was brought from a distance.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KEDAR dark-skinned, the second son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13). It is the name for the nomadic tribes of Arabs, the Bedouins generally (Isaiah 21:16; 42:11; 60:7; Jeremiah 2:10; Ezekiel 27:21), who dwelt in the north-west of Arabia. They lived in black hair-tents (Cant. 1:5). To “dwell in the tents of Kedar” was to be cut off from the worship of the true God (Psalm 120:5). The Kedarites suffered at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 49:28, 29).

The “rams of Nebaioth” (Isaiah 60:7) are the gifts which these wandering tribes of the desert would consecrate to God.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Two nations are in thy womb... and the elder shall serve the younger'. Ephrem reads the womb-oracle Christologically: the two nations are (1) the carnal-old-Israel (the elder, Esau) and (2) the spiritual-new-Israel-in-Christ (the younger, Jacob). The 'elder shall serve younger' inverts natural primogeniture; Tewahedo soteriology preserves Ephrem's reading of this inversion as the foundational pattern: divine election overrides natural-birth order.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Edomites, The, First Born, The.

↩ ◇ Note. Jacob and Esau as nations. The oracle telescopes individuals into peoples — Edom (Esau) and Israel (Jacob). "The older shall serve the younger" — Paul invokes this verse in Romans 9:12 as the paradigm of divine election independent of works. The reversal of birthright primogeniture is a recurring Genesis pattern (Cain/Abel, Ishmael/Isaac, Jacob/Esau, Manasseh/Ephraim, Reuben/Joseph).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MONEY Of uncoined money the first notice we have is in the history of Abraham (Genesis 13:2; 20:16; 24:35). Next, this word is used in connection with the purchase of the cave of Machpelah (23:16), and again in connection with Jacob’s purchase of a field at Shalem (Genesis 33:18, 19) for “an hundred pieces of money”=an hundred Hebrew kesitahs (q.v.), i.e., probably pieces of money, as is supposed, bearing the figure of a lamb. The history of Joseph affords evidence of the constant use of money, silver of a fixed weight. This appears also in all the subsequent history of the Jewish people, in all their internal as well as foreign transactions. There were in common use in trade silver pieces of a definite weight, shekels, half-shekels, and quarter-shekels. But these were not properly coins, which are pieces of metal authoritatively issued, and bearing a stamp. Of the use of coined money we have no early notice among the Hebrews. The first mentioned is of Persian coinage, the daric (Ezra 2:69; Nehemiah 7:70) and the ‘adarkon (Ezra 8:27). The daric (q.v.) was a gold piece current in Palestine in the time of Cyrus. As long as the Jews, after the Exile, lived under Persian rule, they used Persian coins. These gave place to Greek coins when Palestine came under the dominion of the Greeks (B.C. 331), the coins consisting of gold, silver, and copper pieces. The usual gold pieces were staters (q.v.), and the silver coins tetradrachms and drachms. In the year B.C. 140, Antiochus VII. gave permission to Simon the Maccabee to coin Jewish money. Shekels (q.v.) were then coined bearing the figure of the almond rod and the pot of manna.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SILVER used for a great variety of purposes, as may be judged from the frequent references to it in Scripture. It first appears in commerce in Genesis 13:2; 23:15, 16. It was largely employed for making vessels for the sanctuary in the wilderness (Exodus 26:19; 27:17; Numbers 7:13, 19; 10:2). There is no record of its having been found in Syria or Palestine. It was brought in large quantities by foreign merchants from abroad, from Spain and India and other countries probably.

↩ ◇ Note. Abram’s magnanimity. The chapter stages one of the OT’s clearest pictures of patriarchal generosity: Abram, the elder kinsman, has every customary right to first choice of the land but offers Lot the choice instead. The Hebrew anashim aḥim ("we are kinsmen") establishes the theological-relational frame — clan unity outweighs territorial advantage. The contrast with Lot’s subsequent choice (13:10–11, eyes on the well-watered Jordan plain) makes Abram’s self-restraint look retrospectively prudent: Lot ends up in Sodom, while Abram receives unconditional promise of all the land (13:14–17). The narrative encodes one of the patriarchal cycle’s recurring patterns: those who grasp lose, those who release receive. The same theology will return in Jacob’s eventual restoration of Esau’s blessing (33:9–11), in Joseph’s magnanimity to his brothers (50:20), and ultimately in the prophetic critique of land-grasping (Isa 5:8). Abram here is the inaugural model.

↩ ◇ Note. Lot’s fateful choice. The narrator’s aside — "like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt" — is dense with foreshadowing. The comparison to Eden ("the garden of Yahweh") prepares the reader for what follows: a paradise-region that will become the OT’s archetype of catastrophic destruction. The comparison to Egypt is equally pointed: Lot is choosing land like the place his uncle has just escaped (12:10–20), with the same agricultural lushness that makes empires powerful and morally precarious. The narrator’s "before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah" is also chronologically precise: 13:10 is post-destruction perspective inserted into the moment of Lot’s choice, alerting the reader that the landscape Lot is admiring is already, from the narrator’s vantage, ruined. The literary technique is one of Genesis’s most sophisticated — proleptic narrator-comment that reframes a present scene with future knowledge. Lot is choosing what looks like Eden but is in fact future ash.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: GERAR, GERAR, IGNORANCE, IGNORANCE, KADESH.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ABIMELECH my father a king, or father of a king, a common name of the Philistine kings, as “Pharaoh” was of the Egyptian kings. (1.) The Philistine king of Gerar in the time of Abraham (Genesis 20:1-18). By an interposition of Providence, Sarah was delivered from his harem, and was restored to her husband Abraham. As a mark of respect he gave to Abraham valuable gifts, and offered him a settlement in any part of his country; while at the same time he delicately and yet severely rebuked him for having practised a deception upon him in pretending that Sarah was only his sister. Among the gifts presented by the king were a thousand pieces of silver as a “covering of the eyes” for Sarah; i.e., either as an atoning gift and a testimony of her innocence in the sight of all, or rather for the purpose of procuring a veil for Sarah to conceal her beauty, and thus as a reproof to her for not having worn a veil which, as a married woman, she ought to have done. A few years after this Abimelech visited Abraham, who had removed southward beyond his territory, and there entered into a league of peace and friendship with him. This league was the first of which we have any record. It was confirmed by a mutual oath at Beer-sheba (Genesis 21:22-34). (2.) A king of Gerar in the time of Isaac, probably the son of the preceeding (Genesis 26:1-22). Isaac sought refuge in his territory during a famine, and there he acted a part with reference to his wife Rebekah similar to that of his father Abraham with reference to Sarah. Abimelech rebuked him for the deception, which he accidentally discovered. Isaac settled for a while here, and prospered. Abimelech desired him, however, to leave his territory, which Isaac did. Abimelech afterwards visited him when he was encamped at Beer-sheba, and expressed a desire to renew the covenant which had been entered into between their fathers (Genesis 26:26-31). (3.) A son of Gideon (Judges 9:1), who was proclaimed king after the death of his father (Judges 8:33-9:6). One of his first acts was to murder his brothers, seventy in number, “on one stone,” at Ophrah. Only one named Jotham escaped. He was an unprincipled, ambitious ruler, often engaged in war with his own subjects. When engaged in reducing the town of Thebez, which had revolted, he was struck mortally on his head by a mill-stone, thrown by the hand of a woman from the wall above. Perceiving that the wound was mortal, he desired his armour-bearer to thrust him through with his sword, that it might not be said he had perished by the hand of a woman (Judges 9:50-57). (4.) The son of Abiathar, and high priest in the time of David (1 Chronicles 18:16). In the parallel passage, 2 Samuel 8:17, we have the name Ahimelech, and Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech. This most authorities consider the more correct reading. (5.) Achish, king of Gath, in the title of Psalm 34. (Comp. 1 Samuel 21:10-15.)

↩ ◇ Note. The wife-sister theme, again. The episode is the second of three OT wife-sister narratives: Abraham with Pharaoh (Gen 12:10–20), here with Abimelech of Gerar, and Isaac with Abimelech of Gerar (26:6–11). The repetition has been extensively analyzed: source-critically (different documentary sources preserving variant traditions of one event), narratively (escalating pattern in which the patriarchs increasingly grasp Yahweh’s protection without believing they need it), and theologically (Yahweh’s protection of the matriarchal lineage despite patriarchal cowardice). Speiser’s influential 1955 article connected the practice to Hurrian wife-sister legal arrangements at Nuzi, where high-status wives could acquire formal "sister" status to enhance the wife’s legal standing — though most modern scholarship treats this connection as overdrawn. The narratives portray the patriarchs as morally ambiguous: protected by divine intervention despite their deceptions, with foreign rulers occasionally appearing more honorable than the patriarchs themselves (cf. 20:9, Abimelech’s rebuke).

↩ ◇ Note. Abraham as the first prophet. The verse is the OT’s first explicit use of the noun navi ("prophet") for a named individual. Earlier figures (Enoch, Noah) walk with God or are righteous; Abraham is here designated by the technical term that will become one of the central institutional categories of OT religion. The function attached to the title is intercessory ("he will pray for you, and you shall live") — the prophet as the mediator whose prayer can avert the deity’s judgment, the function later operationalized by Moses (Exod 32:11–14), Samuel (1 Sam 12:23), Amos (Amos 7:1–6), and others. The verse establishes prophet-as-intercessor as a primary functional definition of the office, alongside (and prior to) the more familiar prophet-as-message-bearer. The chapter is also unusual in that it portrays Yahweh communicating with a non-Israelite (Abimelech) directly in a dream — registering Yahweh’s reach beyond the patriarchal household even at this early stage of the narrative.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Sarah died... and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her'. Ephrem reads Abraham's mourning as the legitimate-grief warrant: faith in the resurrection does NOT abolish the legitimate human grief at death. Tewahedo funeral theology preserves Ephrem's balance: mourning is permitted (commanded, even) for forty days; Christian hope reshapes mourning but does not eliminate it. Abraham weeping over Sarah's body authorises every Tewahedo funeral weeping.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KIRJATH-ARBA city of Arba, the original name of Hebron (q.v.), so called from the name of its founder, one of the Anakim (Genesis 23:2; 35:27; Joshua 15:13). It was given to Caleb by Joshua as his portion. The Jews interpret the name as meaning “the city of the four”, i.e., of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Adam, who were all, as they allege, buried there.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOURN Frequent references are found in Scripture to, (1.) Mourning for the dead. Abraham mourned for Sarah (Genesis 23:2); Jacob for Joseph (37:34, 35); the Egyptians for Jacob (50:3-10); Israel for Aaron (Numbers 20:29), for Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8), and for Samuel (1 Samuel 25:1); David for Abner (2 Samuel 3:31, 35); Mary and Martha for Lazarus (John 11); devout men for Stephen (Acts 8:2), etc. (2.) For calamities, Job (1:20, 21; 2:8); Israel (Exodus 33:4); the Ninevites (Jonah 3:5); Israel, when defeated by Benjamin (Judges 20:26), etc. (3.) Penitential mourning, by the Israelites on the day of atonement (Leviticus 23:27; Acts 27:9); under Samuel’s ministry (1 Samuel 7:6); predicted in Zechariah (Zechariah 12:10, 11); in many of the psalms (51, etc.). Mourning was expressed, (1) by weeping (Genesis 35:8, marg.; Luke 7:38, etc.); (2) by loud lamentation (Ruth 1:9; 1 Samuel 6:19; 2 Samuel 3:31); (3) by the disfigurement of the person, as rending the clothes (Genesis 37:29, 34; Matthew 26:65), wearing sackcloth (Genesis 37:34; Psalm 35:13), sprinkling dust or ashes on the person (2 Samuel 13:19; Jeremiah 6:26; Job 2:12), shaving the head and plucking out the hair of the head or beard (Leviticus 10:6; Job 1:20), neglect of the person or the removal of ornaments (Exodus 33:4; Deuteronomy 21:12, 13; 2 Samuel 14:2; 19:24; Matthew 6:16, 17), fasting (2 Samuel 1:12), covering the upper lip (Leviticus 13:45; Micah 3:7), cutting the flesh (Jeremiah 16:6, 7), and sitting in silence (Judges 20:26; 2 Samuel 12:16; 13:31; Job 1:20). In the later times we find a class of mourners who could be hired to give by their loud lamentation the external tokens of sorrow (2 Chronicles 35:25; Jeremiah 9:17; Matthew 9:23). The period of mourning for the dead varied. For Jacob it was seventy days (Genesis 50:3); for Aaron (Numbers 20:29) and Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8) thirty days; and for Saul only seven days (1 Samuel 31:13). In 2 Samuel 3:31-35, we have a description of the great mourning for the death of Abner.

↩ ◇ Note. The Hittite recognition. The Hittites of Hebron call Abraham n’si Elohim — "prince of God" or "mighty prince." The phrase recognizes Abraham’s standing as a person of unusual divine favor without using Yahwistic vocabulary; the Hittites speak in their own theological idiom while honoring Abraham. The chapter as a whole is one of the OT’s most carefully observed legal-cultural set pieces: Abraham’s purchase of the cave of Machpelah follows ANE bargaining conventions in detail — repeated demurrals and counter-offers, public witnesses, careful weighing of silver "according to the merchant’s standard" (23:16). Hittite law tablets from Boğazköy preserve the same forms. The result is a legally airtight title to the land that becomes the patriarchal burial ground (Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, Jacob — 49:30–32). Abraham’s only actual property in the promised land at his death is a tomb — the rest of the promise still hangs as future inheritance. The verse and the chapter together establish the deed-of-burial-ground as Israel’s first concrete claim on the land.

↩ ◇ Note. The price of Machpelah. The 400-shekel price is large but not extreme; comparable ANE land-purchase records show prices ranging from a few shekels for small plots to thousands for large estates. The detail "according to the merchant’s standard" (Hebrew over la-soḥer) registers that this is silver weighed by the conventional commercial standard, not coined money — coinage will not appear in the ANE for almost another millennium. The transaction’s scrupulous public character — performed at the city gate, in front of all the Hittites of Hebron — establishes legal title incontestably. Later Genesis episodes in which patriarchs dig wells and have them seized by locals (chs 21, 26) show what happens with informal land-claims; the Machpelah purchase is the secure-title alternative. The chapter is the OT’s clearest single demonstration that the patriarchal family understood property law and operated within it carefully when permanent claim was the goal. Few chapters in Genesis are as legally precise as ch 23.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FAMINE The first mentioned in Scripture was so grievous as to compel Abraham to go down to the land of Egypt (Genesis 26:1). Another is mentioned as having occurred in the days of Isaac, causing him to go to Gerar (Genesis 26:1, 17). But the most remarkable of all was that which arose in Egypt in the days of Joseph, which lasted for seven years (Genesis 41-45). Famines were sent as an effect of God’s anger against a guilty people (2 Kings 8:1, 2; Amos 8:11; Deuteronomy 28:22-42; 2 Samuel 21:1; 2 Kings 6:25-28; 25:3; Jeremiah 14:15; 19:9; 42:17, etc.). A famine was predicted by Agabus (Acts 11:28). Josephus makes mention of the famine which occurred A.D. 45. Helena, queen of Adiabene, being at Jerusalem at that time, procured corn from Alexandria and figs from Cyprus for its poor inhabitants.

↩ ◇ Note Abraham as Torah-keeper. The verse retroactively credits Abraham with keeping all four categories of divine command — voice, requirements (mishmeret), commandments (mitzvot), statutes (chuqqim), laws (torot) — terminology that becomes Torah’s standard vocabulary at Sinai. Rabbinic tradition (m. Kiddushin 4:14) reads this as proof that Abraham kept the entire Torah before it was given. Christian theology has read it differently — Abraham’s “obedience” being faith-trust rather than law-keeping, with Romans 4:13 making faith primary.

↩ ◇ Note. The wife-sister, third occurrence. The third and most ironic of the wife-sister episodes: Abimelech (probably the same king or his successor) discovers the deception not because Yahweh intervenes (as in chs 12 and 20) but because he looks out his window and sees Isaac and Rebekah being affectionate. The Hebrew verb m’tzaḥeq ("caressing, sporting") puns on Isaac’s name (Yitzḥaq, "he laughs") — Isaac is doing what his name describes. The Hebrew wordplay is one of the chapter’s small literary jewels: the name-bearer’s identity-action betrays the deception. Abimelech’s response (26:10–11) is both rebuke and protection: Isaac and Rebekah are now under royal protection rather than royal threat. The episode marks the structural completion of the wife-sister cycle: it begins with Pharaoh’s harem-takeover (12:15), develops with Abimelech’s near-violation (20:6, prevented by divine dream), and resolves with Abimelech’s mature-king response of protection. The narrative arc registers the patriarchal family’s gradual integration into the Levantine political landscape.

An ancient city on the Euphrates (Genesis 36:37; 1 Chronicles 1:48), “Rehoboth by the river.” (3.) Named among the cities of Asshur (Genesis 10:11). Probably, however, the words “rehoboth’ir” are to be translated as in the Vulgate and the margin of A.V., “the streets of the city,” or rather “the public square of the city”, i.e., of Nineveh.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant renewed to Isaac. Yahweh’s appearance to Isaac at Beersheba renews the Abrahamic covenant explicitly — same promise of land, descendants, and blessing — to the second-generation patriarch. The chapter is unusual in being entirely Isaac-centric: he is the only patriarch with no journey out of the land (cf. 26:2–3, where Yahweh forbids him to go to Egypt during famine), making him the most local of the patriarchs. The verse "the God of Abraham your father" inaugurates one of the OT’s most-recurring formulas — "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Exod 3:6, 15, 16, etc.) — that becomes the standard Israelite formula for naming Yahweh by patriarchal ancestry. Jesus’ citation at Matt 22:32 ("God is not the God of the dead, but of the living") makes this verse one of the NT’s key resurrection-proof texts. The chapter is the textual root of the entire later "ancestral God" theology that runs through both testaments.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MOREH an archer, teacher; fruitful. (1.) A Canaanite probably who inhabited the district south of Shechem, between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, and gave his name to the “plain” there (Genesis 12:6). Here at this “plain,” or rather (R.V.) “oak,” of Moreh, Abraham built his first altar in the land of Palestine; and here the Lord appeared unto him. He afterwards left this plain and moved southward, and pitched his tent between Bethel on the west and Hai on the east (Genesis 12:7, 8).

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

First theophany: 'And the Lord appeared unto Abram'. Ephrem emphasises that the Word who appears here is the same Word who became flesh — the Father is invisible, but the Word makes Himself visible through theophanies. The altar Abram builds is the FIRST altar of true worship in the land that will become the holy land, prefiguring every later altar in the Mosaic-Aaronic priesthood and ultimately the Tewahedo tabot. Tewahedo eucharistic theology preserves Ephrem's identification of the OT theophanies as appearances of the pre-incarnate Word.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SOUTH Hebrews Negeb, that arid district to the south of Palestine through which lay the caravan route from Central Palestine to Egypt (Genesis 12:9; 13:1, 3; 46:1-6). “The Negeb comprised a considerable but irregularly-shaped tract of country, its main portion stretching from the mountains and lowlands of Judah in the north to the mountains of Azazemeh in the south, and from the Dead Sea and southern Ghoron the east to the Mediterranean on the west.” In Ezekiel 20:46 (21:1 in Hebrews ) three different Hebrew words are all rendered “south.” (1) “Set thy face toward the south” (Teman, the region on the right, 1 Samuel 33:24); (2) “Drop thy word toward the south” (Negeb, the region of dryness, Joshua 15:4); (3) “Prophesy against the forest of the south field” (Darom, the region of brightness, Deuteronomy 33:23). In Job 37:9 the word “south” is literally “chamber,” used here in the sense of treasury (comp. 38:22; Psalm 135:7). This verse is rendered in the Revised Version “out of the chamber of the south.”

↩ ◇ Note. The first Egyptian sojourn. Abram’s descent to Egypt to escape Canaanite famine establishes a pattern that will recur structurally throughout Genesis and Exodus: famine drives the patriarchal family to Egypt; Egyptian sojourn carries dangers (here, Pharaoh takes Sarai into his harem); divine intervention restores the family to Canaan with augmented wealth (12:16, 20). The pattern recurs almost identically with Isaac (Gen 26, except restricted to Gerar by Yahweh’s explicit prohibition of Egypt) and culminates in Jacob’s descent in chs 46–47, which leads ultimately to Egyptian slavery and the exodus. The chapter functions as a small-scale prefiguration of the entire exodus arc: Sarai threatened in Pharaoh’s house (foreshadowing Israel threatened in Egypt); plagues afflict Pharaoh’s house (12:17, "great plagues"); the family is expelled (12:20, "they sent him away") with Egyptian wealth (12:16). The reader who knows Exodus recognizes the prefigurement: Abram’s small-scale Egyptian episode is the type of Israel’s large-scale Egyptian story.

↩ ◇ Note. Abram’s armed household. The detail that Abram could field 318 trained warriors from his own household registers the size and military character of the patriarchal clan — far larger than the small-family idyll Genesis sometimes seems to portray. The number 318 has an unusual rabbinic afterlife: gematria (the Hebrew letter-numerical system) treats "Eliezer" (Abram’s steward, 15:2) as having numerical value 318, and some early Jewish interpretation reads the verse as Abram going out with Eliezer alone, the entire victory therefore miraculous. The chapter is one of Genesis’s most unusual: Abram as warrior-chief defeating a coalition of four eastern kings (14:1–16), encountering the mysterious Melchizedek (14:18–20), and refusing the king of Sodom’s share of spoils (14:22–24). The chapter’s archaic vocabulary, unusual king-names, and detached relationship to surrounding patriarchal narratives have led many critical scholars (so von Rad) to treat it as preserving very ancient material outside the main documentary sources of Genesis.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And he believed in the Lord; and he counted it to him for righteousness'. Ephrem reads Abraham's faith as the proto-justifying faith — the pattern that Paul will universalise in Rom 4 and Gal 3. Ephrem emphasises that the faith is in a PROMISE (innumerable descendants from a sterile body), not in present visible evidence — establishing faith as TRUST in the divine word against contrary appearance. Tewahedo soteriology preserves the Abrahamic-pattern as the model of saving faith, with Ephrem's emphasis on faith-against-appearance as the monastic-spiritual continuation of this pattern.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GOAT (1.) Hebrews ‘ez, the she-goat (Genesis 15:9; 30:35; 31:38). This Hebrew word is also used for the he-goat (Exodus 12:5; Leviticus 4:23; Numbers 28:15), and to denote a kid (Genesis 38:17, 20). Hence it may be regarded as the generic name of the animal as domesticated. It literally means “strength,” and points to the superior strength of the goat as compared with the sheep. (2.) Hebrews ‘attud, only in plural; rendered “rams” (Genesis 31:10,12); he-goats (Numbers 7:17-88; Isaiah 1:11); goats (Deuteronomy 32:14; Psalm 50:13). They were used in sacrifice (Psalm 66:15). This word is used metaphorically for princes or chiefs in Isaiah 14:9, and in Zechariah 10:3 as leaders. (Comp. Jeremiah 50:8.) (3.) Hebrews gedi, properly a kid. Its flesh was a delicacy among the Hebrews (Genesis 27:9, 14, 17; Judges 6:19). (4.) Hebrews sa’ir, meaning the “shaggy,” a hairy goat, a he-goat (2 Chronicles 29:23); “a goat” (Leviticus 4:24); “satyr” (Isaiah 13:21); “devils” (Leviticus 17:7). It is the goat of the sin-offering (Leviticus 9:3, 15; 10:16). (5.) Hebrews tsaphir, a he-goat of the goats (2 Chronicles 29:21). In Daniel 8:5, 8 it is used as a symbol of the Macedonian empire. (6.) Hebrews tayish, a “striker” or “butter,” rendered “he-goat” (Genesis 30:35; 32:14). (7.) Hebrews ‘azazel (q.v.), the “scapegoat” (Leviticus 16:8, 10,26). (8.) There are two Hebrew words used to denote the undomesticated goat:, Yael, only in plural mountain goats (1 Samuel 24:2; Job 39:1; Psalm 104:18). It is derived from a word meaning “to climb.” It is the ibex, which abounded in the mountainous parts of Moab. And ’akko, only in Deuteronomy 14:5, the wild goat. Goats are mentioned in the New Testament in Matthew 25:32,33; Hebrews 9:12,13, 19; 10:4. They represent oppressors and wicked men (Ezekiel 34:17; 39:18; Matthew 25:33). Several varieties of the goat were familiar to the Hebrews. They had an important place in their rural economy on account of the milk they afforded and the excellency of the flesh of the kid. They formed an important part of pastoral wealth (Genesis 31:10, 12;32:14; 1 Samuel 25:2).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PIGEON Pigeons are mentioned as among the offerings which, by divine appointment, Abram presented unto the Lord (Genesis 15:9). They were afterwards enumerated among the sin-offerings (Leviticus 1:14; 12:6), and the law provided that those who could not offer a lamb might offer two young pigeons (5:7; comp. Luke 2:24). (See DOVE.)

↩ ◇ Note. The territorial promise. The verse defines the Abrahamic land-grant in maximal geographical terms: from the Wadi of Egypt (the river system on the Sinai border, not the Nile itself) to the Euphrates. The territory described is wider than any historical Israelite kingdom ever controlled — even at the height of David and Solomon, the empire reached the Euphrates only briefly through tributary kingdoms. The verse’s ideological function is theologically programmatic: the divine promise exceeds any historical realization, leaving the unfulfilled portion as eschatological surplus. Modern political readings of "biblical Israel’s borders" sometimes appeal to this verse and to Num 34, both of which describe the territorial promise rather than any historical-archaeological reality. The chapter’s preceding ritual — the cutting in two of animals through which Yahweh alone passes (15:10, 17) — is one of the OT’s most unusual covenant ceremonies, transferring all the curse-implications of covenant breach to the deity rather than the human partner. The verse is the ratification of a covenant Yahweh has unilaterally guaranteed.

↩ ◇ Note. The first angel-appearance. The "angel of Yahweh" (Hebrew mal’akh Adonai) appears here for the first time in Genesis — and to Hagar, the Egyptian slave-woman fleeing Sarah’s mistreatment, not to Abraham or Sarah. The episode is theologically remarkable: the first divine messenger encounter goes to a non-Israelite female slave, not to the patriarchal-line. Hagar will subsequently name Yahweh "El-roi" — "the God who sees me" (16:13) — making her the only person in the OT to give a name to God. The chapter is also one of Genesis’s clearest instances of the inner-canonical reversal of expectation: divine attention privileges the marginalized over the established. Phyllis Trible’s reading in Texts of Terror takes Hagar’s narrative as one of the OT’s clearest examples of theological literature giving voice and dignity to the structurally voiceless. The verse opens one of the patriarchal cycle’s most morally and theologically complex sub-narratives.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant of circumcision. The command institutes the practice that becomes the OT’s most distinctive single physical marker of covenant identity. Circumcision was practiced in many ANE cultures (Egypt, the Levant, parts of Mesopotamia) but typically as a puberty-rite or marriage-preparation; Israelite uniqueness is the eighth-day-after-birth timing (17:12) and the explicit theological framing as covenant sign rather than social-developmental rite. The practice becomes definitive of Jewish identity, contested in NT theology (Acts 15, the Jerusalem Council; Galatians on Paul’s apostolic-era debate over Gentile circumcision), and re-spiritualized as "circumcision of the heart" (Deut 10:16, 30:6, Jer 4:4, Rom 2:28–29). The verse is one of the OT’s most institutionally durable provisions; circumcision continues as primary Jewish identity-marker into the present. The chapter as a whole is also Abram’s name-change to Abraham, marking the covenant moment with both somatic (circumcision) and onomastic (renaming) signs.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). COOK a person employed to perform culinary service. In early times among the Hebrews cooking was performed by the mistress of the household (Genesis 18:2-6; Judges 6:19), and the process was very expeditiously performed (Genesis 27:3, 4, 9, 10). Professional cooks were afterwards employed (1 Samuel 8:13; 9:23). Few animals, as a rule, were slaughtered (other than sacrifices), except for purposes of hospitality (Genesis 18:7; Luke 15:23). The paschal lamb was roasted over a fire (Exodus 12:8, 9; 2Chronicles 35:13). Cooking by boiling was the usual method adopted (Leviticus 8:31; Exodus 16:23). No cooking took place on the Sabbath day (Exodus 35:3).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BAKE The duty of preparing bread was usually, in ancient times, committed to the females or the slaves of the family (Genesis 18:6; Leviticus 26:26; 1 Samuel 8:13); but at a later period we find a class of public bakers mentioned (Hos. 7:4, 6; Jeremiah 37:21). The bread was generally in the form of long or round cakes (Exodus 29:23; 1 Samuel 2:36), of a thinness that rendered them easily broken (Isaiah 58:7; Matthew 14:19; 26:26; Acts 20:11). Common ovens were generally used; at other times a jar was half-filled with hot pebbles, and the dough was spread over them. Hence we read of “cakes baken on the coals” (1 Kings 19:6), and “baken in the oven” (Leviticus 2:4). (See BREAD.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FLOUR Grain reduced to the form of meal is spoken of in the time of Abraham (Genesis 18:6). As baking was a daily necessity, grain was also ground daily at the mills (Jeremiah 25:10). The flour mingled with water was kneaded in kneading-troughs, and sometimes leaven (Exodus 12:34) was added and sometimes omitted (Genesis 19:3). The dough was then formed into thin cakes nine or ten inches in diameter and baked in the oven. Fine flour was offered by the poor as a sin-offering (Leviticus 5:11-13), and also in connection with other sacrifices (Numbers 15:3-12; 28:7-29).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). KNEAD to prepare dough in the process of baking (Genesis 18:6; 1 Samuel 28:24; Hos. 7:4).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MILL for grinding corn, mentioned as used in the time of Abraham (Genesis 18:6). That used by the Hebrews consisted of two circular stones, each 2 feet in diameter and half a foot thick, the lower of which was called the “nether millstone” (Job 41:24) and the upper the “rider.” The upper stone was turned round by a stick fixed in it as a handle. There were then no public mills, and thus each family required to be provided with a hand-mill. The corn was ground daily, generally by the women of the house (Isaiah 47:1, 2; Matthew 24:41). It was with the upper stone of a hand-mill that “a certain woman” at Thebez broke Abimelech’s skull (Judges 9:53, “a piece of a millstone;” literally, “a millstone rider”, i.e., the “runner,” the stone which revolves. Comp. 2 Samuel 11:21). Millstones could not be pledged (Deuteronomy 24:6), as they were necessary in every family.

↩ ◇ Note. The rhetorical question. The visitor’s question (Hebrew ha-yiplah me-Adonai davar) becomes one of the OT’s most-quoted single lines in subsequent biblical literature: Jer 32:17, 27 ("nothing is too hard for you"), Zech 8:6, Luke 1:37 (the angel’s assurance to Mary, "with God nothing is impossible," in nearly direct allusion to this verse). The question is rhetorical only because the answer is presupposed; it functions theologically as a foundational claim about divine capability. The verse’s literary placement is significant: Sarah has just laughed at the announcement that she will conceive at age 90 (18:12), and the question both rebukes her skepticism and invites her into trust. The chapter’s entire scene — three visitors, hospitality at Mamre, the announcement of Isaac’s conception — has had unusual interpretive history: Christian tradition (especially Eastern Orthodox icons of the "Hospitality of Abraham") has read the three visitors as Trinitarian theophany, with Andrei Rublev’s 15th-century icon making this verse-cluster one of the most-depicted scenes in iconographic tradition.

↩ ◇ Note. The blinding of the Sodomites. The angels protect Lot’s household from the assault by striking the besiegers blind — preserving the immediate physical threat from materializing while also functioning as theological signal: the Sodomites cannot see what is in front of them in any sense, sensory or moral. The Hebrew sanverim ("dazzling-blindness," from a root meaning "to flash") suggests not ordinary blindness but sudden disorienting flash — the same word will recur at 2 Kgs 6:18 (Elisha’s blinding of the Aramean army). The chapter as a whole is one of the OT’s most morally agonizing texts: Lot’s offer of his daughters in place of the angels (19:8) registers a depth of patriarchal distortion that the narrator records without comment. Many feminist readings (so Phyllis Trible, J. Cheryl Exum) have engaged this episode as one of the most disturbing in the OT — the host’s offering of vulnerable family members for the protection of male guests is theological-ethical horror, and the chapter frames it within the larger horror of Sodom that produces it.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HEIR Under the patriarchs the property of a father was divided among the sons of his legitimate wives (Genesis 21:10; 24:36; 25:5), the eldest son getting a larger portion than the rest. The Mosaic law made specific regulations regarding the transmission of real property, which are given in detail in Deuteronomy 21:17; Numbers 27:8; 36:6; 27:9-11. Succession to property was a matter of right and not of favour. Christ is the “heir of all things” (Hebrews 1:2; Colossians 1:15). Believers are heirs of the “promise,” “of righteousness,” “of the kingdom,” “of the world,” “of God,” “joint heirs” with Christ (Gal 3:29; Hebrews 6:17; 11:7; James 2:5; Romans 4:13; 8:17).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). WELL (Hebrews beer), to be distinguished from a fountain (Hebrews ‘ain). A “beer” was a deep shaft, bored far under the rocky surface by the art of man, which contained water which percolated through the strata in its sides. Such wells were those of Jacob and Beersheba, etc. (see Genesis 21:19, 25, 30, 31; 24:11; 26:15, 18-25, 32, etc.). In the Pentateuch this word beer, so rendered, occurs twenty-five times.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BOW The bow was in use in early times both in war and in the chase (Genesis 21:20; 27:3; 48:22). The tribe of Benjamin were famous for the use of the bow (1 Chronicles 8:40; 12:2; 2 Chronicles 14:8; 17:17); so also were the Elamites (Isaiah 22:6) and the Lydians (Jeremiah 46:9). The Hebrew word commonly used for bow means properly to tread (1 Chronicles 5:18; 8:40), and hence it is concluded that the foot was employed in bending the bow. Bows of steel (correctly “copper”) are mentioned (2 Samuel 22:35; Psalm 18:34). The arrows were carried in a quiver (Genesis 27:3; Isaiah 22:6; 49:2; Psalm 127:5). They were apparently sometimes shot with some burning material attached to them (Psalm 120:4). The bow is a symbol of victory (Psalm 7:12). It denotes also falsehood, deceit (Psalm 64:3, 4; Hos. 7:16; Jeremiah 9:3). “The use of the bow” in 2 Samuel 1:18 (A.V.) ought to be “the song of the bow,” as in the Revised Version.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PARAN abounding in foliage, or abounding in caverns, (Genesis 21:21), a desert tract forming the north-eastern division of the peninsula of Sinai, lying between the ‘Arabah on the east and the wilderness of Shur on the west. It is intersected in a north-western direction by the Wady el-‘Arish. It bears the modern name of Badiet et-Tih, i.e., “the desert of the wanderings.” This district, through which the children of Israel wandered, lay three days’ march from Sinai (Numbers 10:12, 33). From Kadesh, in this wilderness, spies (q.v.) were sent to spy the land (13:3, 26). Here, long afterwards, David found refuge from Saul (1 Samuel 25:1, 4).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEERSHEBA well of the oath, or well of seven, a well dug by Abraham, and so named because he and Abimelech here entered into a compact (Genesis 21:31). On re-opening it, Isaac gave it the same name (Genesis 26:31-33). It was a favourite place of abode of both of these patriarchs (21:33-22:1, 19; 26:33; 28:10). It is mentioned among the “cities” given to the tribe of Simeon (Joshua 19:2; 1 Chronicles 4:28). From Dan to Beersheba, a distance of about 144 miles (Judges 20:1; 1 Chronicles 21:2; 2 Samuel 24:2), became the usual way of designating the whole Promised Land, and passed into a proverb. After the return from the Captivity the phrase is narrowed into “from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom” (Nehemiah 11:30). The kingdom of the ten tribes extended from Beersheba to Mount Ephraim (2 Chronicles 19:4). The name is not found in the New Testament. It is still called by the Arabs Bir es-Seba, i.e., “well of the seven”, where there are to the present day two principal wells and five smaller ones. It is nearly midway between the southern end of the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean.

↩ ◇ Note. The tamarisk and the well. Abraham plants a tamarisk tree at Beersheba and "called there on the name of Yahweh, the Everlasting God" (Hebrew El Olam). The detail is one of Genesis’s small archaeological-cultic windows: tree-planting at well-sites was a recognized form of patriarchal-period sacred-space marking, with the tree functioning as visible long-term identifier of the encounter. The same pattern recurs elsewhere (the oak of Mamre, the oak of Moreh) — patriarchal "altars" in the loose sense were often actually trees, wells, or stones, marking sites where divine encounter had occurred. The "Everlasting God" name is theologically significant: El Olam identifies Yahweh with permanence-eternity beyond the patriarchal family’s ephemeral existence. The chapter as a whole is also significant for the well-rights treaty between Abraham and Abimelech (21:22–32) — one of Genesis’s clearest portraits of patriarchal-era diplomacy in the Negev. The tamarisk and the well together encode a recurring patriarchal-period cultic-political pattern.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering'. Ephrem reads this verse as the most direct prophecy of the Crucifixion in the entire Torah: God will provide HIMSELF (i.e., God-incarnate) as the lamb. The substitution-of-ram (22:13) is a temporal stay; the ultimate lamb is the God-man on the Cross. Tewahedo Christology preserves Ephrem's reading: the ram caught in the thicket prefigures Christ's crown of thorns; Isaac unbound prefigures the empty tomb.

↩ ◇ Note. The servant’s prayer. Abraham’s anonymous servant (traditionally identified with Eliezer of Damascus, 15:2) prays for explicit divine guidance in finding a wife for Isaac, then constructs a specific test (24:13–14): the woman who offers to draw water for him and his camels will be Yahweh’s choice. The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest portraits of divinely-guided decision-making through prayer-test (the same pattern recurs with Gideon’s fleece, Judg 6:36–40). The servant’s prayer is also significant for invoking ḥesed ("steadfast love, covenant kindness") as both what he asks Yahweh to show Abraham (24:12) and what defines Rebekah’s response (24:14, the unprompted offering to water all the camels — an enormous quantity of water for a stranger). The chapter is the OT’s longest single chapter on a marital-arrangement, and its detail registers the theological-political importance of finding the right covenant-line wife. Rebekah’s eagerness to leave home immediately (24:58, "I will go") mirrors Abraham’s leaving in 12:1 — both are summoned by promise into unknown terrain.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ESAU hairy, Rebekah’s first-born twin son (Genesis 25:25). The name of Edom, “red”, was also given to him from his conduct in connection with the red lentil “pottage” for which he sold his birthright (30, 31). The circumstances connected with his birth foreshadowed the enmity which afterwards subsisted between the twin brothers and the nations they founded (25:22, 23, 26). In process of time Jacob, following his natural bent, became a shepherd; while Esau, a “son of the desert,” devoted himself to the perilous and toilsome life of a huntsman. On a certain occasion, on returning from the chase, urged by the cravings of hunger, Esau sold his birthright to his brother, Jacob, who thereby obtained the covenant blessing (Genesis 27:28, 29, 36; Hebrews 12:16, 17). He afterwards tried to regain what he had so recklessly parted with, but was defeated in his attempts through the stealth of his brother (Genesis 27:4, 34, 38). At the age of forty years, to the great grief of his parents, he married (Genesis 26:34, 35) two Canaanitish maidens, Judith, the daughter of Beeri, and Bashemath, the daughter of Elon. When Jacob was sent away to Padan-aram, Esau tried to conciliate his parents (Genesis 28:8, 9) by marrying his cousin Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael. This led him to cast in his lot with the Ishmaelite tribes; and driving the Horites out of Mount Seir, he settled in that region. After some thirty years’ sojourn in Padan-aram Jacob returned to Canaan, and was reconciled to Esau, who went forth to meet him (33:4). Twenty years after this, Isaac their father died, when the two brothers met, probably for the last time, beside his grave (35:29). Esau now permanently left Canaan, and established himself as a powerful and wealthy chief in the land of Edom (q.v.). Long after this, when the descendants of Jacob came out of Egypt, the Edomites remembered the old quarrel between the brothers, and with fierce hatred they warred against Israel.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: Children.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: ESAU, ISAAC, JACOB, REBEKAH (REBECCA), TWINS.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JACOB one who follows on another’s heels; supplanter, (Genesis 25:26; 27:36; Hos. 12:2-4), the second born of the twin sons of Isaac by Rebekah. He was born probably at Lahai-roi, when his father was fifty-nine and Abraham one hundred and fifty-nine years old. Like his father, he was of a quiet and gentle disposition, and when he grew up followed the life of a shepherd, while his brother Esau became an enterprising hunter. His dealing with Esau, however, showed much mean selfishness and cunning (Genesis 25:29-34). When Isaac was about 160 years of age, Jacob and his mother conspired to deceive the aged patriarch (Genesis 27), with the view of procuring the transfer of the birthright to himself. The birthright secured to him who possessed it (1) superior rank in his family (Genesis 49:3); (2) a double portion of the paternal inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17); (3) the priestly office in the family (Numbers 8:17-19); and (4) the promise of the Seed in which all nations of the earth were to be blessed (Genesis 22:18). Soon after his acquisition of his father’s blessing (Genesis 27), Jacob became conscious of his guilt; and afraid of the anger of Esau, at the suggestion of Rebekah Isaac sent him away to Haran, 400 miles or more, to find a wife among his cousins, the family of Laban, the Syrian (28). There he met with Rachel (29). Laban would not consent to give him his daughter in marriage till he had served seven years; but to Jacob these years “seemed but a few days, for the love he had to her.” But when the seven years were expired, Laban craftily deceived Jacob, and gave him his daughter Leah. Other seven years of service had to be completed probably before he obtained the beloved Rachel. But “life-long sorrow, disgrace, and trials, in the retributive providence of God, followed as a consequence of this double union.” At the close of the fourteen years of service, Jacob desired to return to his parents, but at the entreaty of Laban he tarried yet six years with him, tending his flocks (31:41). He then set out with his family and property “to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan” (Genesis 31). Laban was angry when he heard that Jacob had set out on his journey, and pursued after him, overtaking him in seven days. The meeting was of a painful kind. After much recrimination and reproach directed against Jacob, Laban is at length pacified, and taking an affectionate farewell of his daughters, returns to his home in Padanaram. And now all connection of the Israelites with Mesopotamia is at an end. Soon after parting with Laban he is met by a company of angels, as if to greet him on his return and welcome him back to the Land of Promise (32:1, 2). He called the name of the place Mahanaim, i.e., “the double camp,” probably his own camp and that of the angels. The vision of angels was the counterpart of that he had formerly seen at Bethel, when, twenty years before, the weary, solitary traveller, on his way to Padan-aram, saw the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder whose top reached to heaven (28:12). He now hears with dismay of the approach of his brother Esau with a band of 400 men to meet him. In great agony of mind he prepares for the worst. He feels that he must now depend only on God, and he betakes himself to him in earnest prayer, and sends on before him a munificent present to Esau, “a present to my Lord Esau from thy servant Jacob.” Jacob’s family were then transported across the Jabbok; but he himself remained behind, spending the night in communion with God. While thus engaged, there appeared one in the form of a man who wrestled with him. In this mysterious contest Jacob prevailed, and as a memorial of it his name was changed to Israel (wrestler with God); and the place where this occured he called Peniel, “for”, said he, “I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved” (32:25-31). After this anxious night, Jacob went on his way, halting, mysteriously weakened by the conflict, but strong in the assurance of the divine favour. Esau came forth and met him; but his spirit of revenge was appeased, and the brothers met as friends, and during the remainder of their lives they maintained friendly relations. After a brief sojourn at Succoth, Jacob moved forward and pitched his tent near Shechem (q.v.), 33:18; but at length, under divine directions, he moved to Bethel, where he made an altar unto God (35:6,7), and where God appeared to him and renewed the Abrahamic covenant. While journeying from Bethel to Ephrath (the Canaanitish name of Bethlehem), Rachel died in giving birth to her second son Benjamin (35:16-20), fifteen or sixteen years after the birth of Joseph. He then reached the old family residence at Mamre, to wait on the dying bed of his father Isaac. The complete reconciliation between Esau and Jacob was shown by their uniting in the burial of the patriarch (35:27-29). Jacob was soon after this deeply grieved by the loss of his beloved son Joseph through the jealousy of his brothers (37:33). Then follows the story of the famine, and the successive goings down into Egypt to buy corn (42), which led to the discovery of the long-lost Joseph, and the patriarch’s going down with all his household, numbering about seventy souls (Exodus 1:5; Deuteronomy 10:22; Acts 7:14), to sojourn in the land of Goshen. Here Jacob, “after being strangely tossed about on a very rough ocean, found at last a tranquil harbour, where all the best affections of his nature were gently exercised and largely unfolded” (Genesis 48). At length the end of his checkered course draws nigh, and he summons his sons to his bedside that he may bless them. Among his last words he repeats the story of Rachel’s death, although forty years had passed away since that event took place, as tenderly as if it had happened only yesterday; and when “he had made an end of charging his sons, he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the ghost” (49:33). His body was embalmed and carried with great pomp into the land of Canaan, and buried beside his wife Leah in the cave of Machpelah, according to his dying charge. There, probably, his embalmed body remains to this day (50:1-13). (See HEBRON.) The history of Jacob is referred to by the prophets Hosea (12:3, 4, 12) and Malachi (1:2). In Micah 1:5 the name is a poetic synonym for Israel, the kingdom of the ten tribes. There are, besides the mention of his name along with those of the other patriarchs, distinct references to events of his life in Paul’s epistles (Romans 9:11-13; Hebrews 12:16; 11:21). See references to his vision at Bethel and his possession of land at Shechem in John 1:51; 4:5, 12; also to the famine which was the occasion of his going down into Egypt in Acts 7:12 (See LUZ; BETHEL.)

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: First Born, The.

↩ ◇ Note. The sale of the birthright. The episode that frames Jacob and Esau’s lifelong contest: Esau, returning starving from a hunt, sells his birthright (the elder son’s double-portion inheritance and clan-leadership) to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. The narrator’s dismissive characterization of Esau — "thus Esau despised his birthright" (25:34) — provides the theological evaluation: the failure is Esau’s, not Jacob’s coercion. The chapter also generates the name "Edom" ("red," from the red stew) as Esau’s alternate name and his descendants’ ethnic designation. Heb 12:16 cites this episode as the OT example of profanity ("godlessness"), Esau as the archetypal person who trades a permanent good for an immediate appetite. The chapter is also significant for Yahweh’s prenatal oracle to Rebekah (25:23, "the elder shall serve the younger") — the divine choice precedes either twin’s action and sets up the entire Genesis pattern of younger-over-older election that the chapter will work out narratively. Paul cites this oracle at Rom 9:11–13 in his discussion of divine election prior to human merit.

↩ ◇ Note. Why Cain’s offering was rejected. The text gives no explicit reason for the differential acceptance of Abel’s offering over Cain’s. Three interpretive traditions divide the question: (1) Abel offered the firstborn from his flock and the fat — the choicest portion — while Cain offered “fruit of the ground” without specifying first-fruits or quality (the Hebrew is silent on Cain’s “first,” explicit on Abel’s bekhorot); (2) the difference is in the offerers’ inner state, the reading Hebrews 11:4 takes (“by faith Abel offered…”); (3) the rejection is sovereign election, with no condition attached (Calvin, Institutes 3.21). Hebrews and 1 John 3:12 (“his deeds were evil”) attach moral weight to Cain rather than to the offering form.

↩ ◇ Note. Cursed from the ground. The ground (adamah, the same word as “Adam”) is the curse’s pivot — it “opens its mouth to receive your brother’s blood.” This anthropomorphizing of the earth as moral witness recurs in Job 16:18 (“O earth, do not cover my blood”), Numbers 35:33 (bloodshed pollutes the land), and Isaiah 26:21. The motif culminates in Hebrews 12:24 (“the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel”) — Abel’s blood cries for vengeance, Christ’s blood for forgiveness. The contrast is one of the New Testament’s most explicit reuses of Genesis 4.

↩ ◇ Note. Cain as civilization-founder. Cain — the murderer, the wanderer, the cursed — becomes the founder of urban civilization. The juxtaposition of Cain’s cursing as wanderer (4:12) with his city-building (4:17) is theologically loaded. Augustine’s City of God (XV.5) uses this passage to articulate his “two cities” doctrine: the earthly city begins with Cain, the heavenly city with Abel and the line of Seth. Later urban-theological strands (Ellul’s The Meaning of the City, 1970) read this verse as making cities ambivalent: human achievement built atop human violence, productive but unredeemed.

↩ ◇ Note. Image transmitted through Adam. The image-and-likeness language of 1:26–27 is here applied to Seth as Adam’s son — pointedly NOT to Cain (5:3 follows the Cain genealogy of ch 4 and reorients to Seth). Some commentators read this as deliberate exclusion: the divine image transmits through Seth’s line, not Cain’s. The Hebrew syntax (in his own likeness, after his image) inverts the order of 1:26 (in our image, after our likeness) — Adam transmits in reverse what God bestowed. The Imago Dei thus carries not only theological but genealogical implications: the line through which it passes becomes the line of promise (Seth → Noah → Abraham → David).

↩ ◇ Note. Antediluvian longevity. The pre-flood patriarchs’ lifespans (Adam 930, Methuselah 969, Jared 962) parallel the Sumerian King List, which records eight to ten antediluvian kings reigning 18,600 to 43,200 years each. Both traditions distinguish a primordial age of extraordinary longevity from the historical present. Three interpretive options dominate modern scholarship: literal historical (lifespans gradually shortened by environmental or divine factors); symbolic-numerological (the ages encode mathematical or sexagesimal patterns); or genealogical-compressive (figures represent lineages, not individuals). Sailhamer emphasizes that all the patriarchs nevertheless died, against Eden’s apparent promise — death’s universality is the chapter’s main point.

↩ ◇ Note. “When he dies, it sends.” The name Methuselah (מְתוּשֶׁלַח) has been variously etymologized as “man of the dart/weapon” or, in a popular reading, “when he dies, it [the flood] sends.” The numerical structure supports the latter: Methuselah was 187 when Lamech was born, Lamech 182 when Noah was born, Noah 600 at the flood — totaling exactly 969, Methuselah’s lifespan (5:27). The Sethite line’s longest-living patriarch dies in the very year of the flood. Whether this is intentional naming or post-hoc numerology is debated, but the textual coincidence is striking enough that many ancient and modern interpreters have read it as deliberate.
